title: Web3 Networking & Building Connections Guide
subtitle: Master the Art of Building Meaningful Relationships in Web3

intro.title: Why Connections Matter in Web3
intro.content:
In Web3, your network isn't just important—it's often the difference between success and obscurity. Unlike traditional industries where credentials and experience dominate, Web3 moves at breakneck speed. The best opportunities often come from knowing the right people at the right time.

This isn't about collecting followers or connections like trading cards. It's about building genuine, mutually beneficial relationships with founders, investors, developers, and researchers who can help you grow—and whom you can help in return.

The Web3 ecosystem is built on trust and reputation in a pseudonymous world. A warm introduction from a respected community member carries more weight than any resume. In this guide, you'll learn how to systematically build a network that opens doors, creates opportunities, and helps you contribute meaningfully to the ecosystem.

finding_people.title: Finding Key People to Connect With
finding_people.content: Before you can build relationships, you need to know who to connect with. Web3 networking isn't about reaching out to everyone—it's about identifying the right people who align with your interests, goals, and values.

identifying_targets.title: Identifying Who to Connect With
identifying_targets.content:
Different types of key people in Web3:

  • Founders and Builders: People actively building projects. They're great for learning, collaboration, and potential hiring opportunities
  • Investors (VCs and Angels): If you're building, these connections are crucial for fundraising. But build the relationship before you need money
  • Developers and Researchers: Technical experts who can provide deep insights and collaboration opportunities
  • Community Leaders: People who organize events, moderate communities, and connect others
  • Ecosystem Contributors: Writers, educators, and content creators who help grow the space

How to prioritize: Start with people in your specific niche (DeFi, NFTs, infrastructure, etc.). It's better to be deeply connected in one area than superficially connected across everything.

research.title: Research Before Reaching Out
research.content:
Never reach out cold without doing your homework. The 5-minute research rule: Before contacting someone, spend at least 5 minutes understanding:

  • What they're currently working on or interested in
  • Their recent tweets, blog posts, or public statements
  • Projects they've funded, built, or advised
  • Their pain points or challenges (mentioned in tweets/interviews)
  • Mutual connections you share

Tools for research:

  • Twitter/X: Read their recent tweets and replies (not just their main timeline)
  • LinkedIn: Check their professional background and connections
  • GitHub: See what they're contributing to
  • Podcast appearances and conference talks
  • Past investments or advisory roles

understanding_interests.title: Understanding Their Interests and Work
understanding_interests.content:
Generic outreach fails. Personalized outreach based on genuine interest succeeds. When you reach out, you should be able to reference:

  • Specific work: "I saw your research on optimistic rollups" beats "I like your work"
  • Recent developments: "Congrats on the recent funding round" shows you're paying attention
  • Shared interests: "I'm also fascinated by MEV" creates common ground
  • Thoughtful questions: Questions that show you've thought deeply about their work

Example: Instead of "Can I pick your brain about DeFi?", try "I read your article on Curve's tricrypto pools and have a question about the dynamic fee mechanism—would you be open to a quick chat?"

twitter_strategies.title: Twitter Lists and Following Strategies
twitter_strategies.content:
Twitter is Web3's town square. Mastering it is essential for discovering and tracking key people.

Create organized Twitter lists:

  • "VCs I Follow" - Track investor thoughts and what they're excited about
  • "Builders in [Your Niche]" - Stay updated on what's being built
  • "Researchers" - Learn from the smartest technical minds
  • "Potential Collaborators" - People you might want to work with

Engagement strategy:

  1. Follow 50-100 key people in your niche (don't follow thousands indiscriminately)
  2. Turn on notifications for 5-10 most important accounts
  3. Engage authentically with their content—add value, don't just say "gm"
  4. Quote tweet with your insights (not just retweet)
  5. Reply early to their questions (when you have genuine answers)

Building visibility: When someone consistently sees thoughtful replies from you, you're no longer a stranger when you DM them.

first_contact.title: Making First Contact
first_contact.content: The first message sets the tone for the entire relationship. Get it right, and you open a door. Get it wrong, and you get ignored—or worse, remembered for the wrong reasons.

cold_dm_strategies.title: Cold DM Strategies That Work
cold_dm_strategies.content:
The anatomy of a good cold DM:

  1. Personalized opening: Reference something specific about them
  2. Establish credibility: Brief context about who you are
  3. Clear ask: Be specific about what you want
  4. Make it easy: Low commitment, easy to respond to
  5. Value proposition: What's in it for them?

Example DM Template (Good):
"Hey [Name], I saw your thread about MEV on L2s—the point about cross-domain arbitrage was fascinating. I've been researching similar dynamics for [Project]. Would you be open to a 15-min call? I'd love to share what I've found and get your thoughts. Happy to send my research doc first."

Why this works:

  • Shows you read their work (specific reference)
  • Establishes you're working on something relevant
  • Clear, bounded ask (15 minutes, not "pick your brain")
  • Offers value first (sharing research)
  • Makes it easy to say yes or no

what_not_to_do.title: Common Cold Outreach Mistakes
what_not_to_do.content:
Don't do these things:

  • "Can I pick your brain?" - Vague and sounds like you want to take without giving
  • "I'd love to learn from you" - Generic and offers no value
  • Long life story in first message - Nobody has time for a 500-word DM from a stranger
  • "Check out my project" - This is spam unless you have a very specific reason they'd care
  • Asking for intro to their network immediately - Build the relationship first
  • Generic template that clearly went to 100 people - "Dear founder" is an instant delete
  • Sending during busy conference weeks - They're getting 100+ DMs, yours will be lost

The biggest mistake: Asking before giving. Always think "How can I provide value first?" even if it's just a thoughtful perspective or useful information.

value_first.title: Providing Value First Approach
value_first.content:
The most powerful networking strategy: give before you ask. When you provide value upfront, people naturally want to help you back.

Ways to provide value:

  • Share relevant research or articles: "Saw this paper on ZK-SNARKs, thought you'd find it interesting given your work on [X]"
  • Make useful introductions: Connect people in your network who could benefit from knowing each other
  • Contribute to their project: Submit a thoughtful GitHub issue, write documentation, or create content
  • Answer their questions publicly: When they ask on Twitter, provide a helpful response
  • Promote their work: Share their content with genuine commentary explaining why it's valuable
  • Provide beta testing or feedback: Offer to test their product and give detailed, constructive feedback

Real example: A developer wanted to connect with a prominent DeFi founder. Instead of asking for a job, he found a bug in their documentation, submitted a detailed PR fixing it, and then reached out: "Fixed a few issues in your docs—happy to help further if useful." Result: conversation started, relationship built, job offer came months later.

warm_intros.title: Warm Introductions and Mutual Connections
warm_intros.content:
A warm introduction from a mutual connection is 10x more effective than a cold DM. Always look for the warm path first.

How to get warm intros:

  1. Map your network: Who do you know who might know them?
  2. Check mutual connections: LinkedIn and Twitter both show mutual connections
  3. Ask in the right way: Don't just say "Can you intro me to X?"
  4. Make it easy for the connector: Provide context and draft the intro email yourself

The double opt-in intro: The gold standard. Your mutual connection asks person B: "Would you be open to an intro to [your name] who is working on [X]?" Only after B says yes does the intro happen.

Template for asking for an intro:
"Hey [Connector], I'm working on [specific thing] and would love to talk to [Target] about [specific topic]. I know you know them—would you be comfortable making an introduction? No pressure if not, I can reach out cold. If yes, I've drafted a quick intro email below to make it easy: [Draft]"

Draft intro to provide:
"[Target], meet [Your name] who is working on [X]. [One sentence about why you two should connect]. [Your name], [Target] is the expert on [Y] and built [Z]. I thought you two should know each other."

email_outreach.title: Email Outreach Best Practices
email_outreach.content:
Email is less common in Web3 than DMs, but it's still important for formal introductions, investor outreach, and partnership discussions.

Email structure that works:

  1. Subject line: Specific and intriguing. "Quick question about [specific topic]" or "Intro from [Mutual Contact]"
  2. First sentence: Why you're reaching out (the hook)
  3. Second paragraph: Brief context about you (2-3 sentences max)
  4. Third paragraph: Specific ask or value proposition
  5. Close: Make next step clear and easy

Example email:
Subject: Question about cross-chain messaging security

Hi [Name],

I recently read your research on cross-chain bridge exploits and your proposed security framework really resonated with the challenges we're facing at [Project].

Quick context: I'm the lead developer at [Project], working on [specific technical challenge]. We're building [one-sentence description].

I'd love to get 20 minutes of your time to discuss how your framework might apply to our architecture. I've already implemented the initial threat model and would value your feedback.

Would you be open to a call next week? I'm flexible on timing.

Best,
[Your name]

Follow-up strategy: If no response in 5-7 days, send one polite follow-up. If still no response, move on. Don't be that person who sends 5 follow-ups.

building_relationships.title: Building Genuine Relationships
building_relationships.content: Getting a response is just the beginning. The real skill is turning a single interaction into a lasting, mutually beneficial relationship.

connection_to_relationship.title: From Connection to Relationship
connection_to_relationship.content:
A connection becomes a relationship through repeated, valuable interactions over time. You can't force it—but you can create the conditions for it.

Stages of relationship depth:

  1. Awareness: They know who you are
  2. Recognition: They remember you when they see your name
  3. Active connection: You exchange value occasionally
  4. Relationship: You stay in touch regularly and think of each other
  5. Partnership/Friendship: Deep mutual trust and collaboration

Moving through stages: Each interaction should add value. After your first conversation, find a reason for a second one that benefits both of you. After meeting at a conference, follow up with something relevant to your conversation. Consistency and value move relationships forward.

The time factor: Real relationships take months or years. Don't rush. Someone you meet casually today might become a co-founder in two years. Play the long game.

following_up.title: Following Up Without Being Annoying
following_up.content:
Following up is essential. Being annoying is fatal. Here's how to do it right:

When to follow up:

  • After meeting at an event (within 24-48 hours)
  • After a helpful conversation (to share results or say thanks)
  • When you have something valuable to share with them
  • When you come across something relevant to a past conversation
  • Every 1-3 months to maintain the relationship (for important connections)

When NOT to follow up:

  • Daily or weekly without new value
  • After they've ignored 2+ messages
  • Just to "check in" with nothing to offer
  • To ask for another favor immediately after they helped you

Good follow-up examples:

  • "Hey! That strategy you suggested worked—we saw 40% improvement. Thank you!"
  • "Saw this research paper on [topic we discussed], thought you'd find it relevant"
  • "Update: we shipped the feature we talked about. Would love your feedback"
  • "Met someone working on similar problems—happy to make an intro if useful"

The reciprocity rule: For every ask, provide value 3 times. If someone helps you once, help them three times before asking again.

offering_help.title: Offering Help and Value
offering_help.content:
The best networkers are the best givers. When you genuinely help others succeed, they naturally want to help you.

Ways to provide ongoing value:

  • Make introductions: Connect people in your network who would benefit from knowing each other
  • Share opportunities: Forward relevant job postings, grants, speaking opportunities
  • Provide feedback: Offer thoughtful product feedback, review pitches, or beta test
  • Amplify their work: Share their content, write testimonials, or provide case studies
  • Share knowledge: Write tutorials, create content, or answer questions in your area of expertise
  • Offer your skills: Design work, code review, writing help—whatever you're good at

The "give without expectation" mindset: Help people even when they can't help you back right now. Maybe they never will. Do it anyway. This is how you build real reputation and karma in Web3.

Real story: A designer spent weekends creating free brand assets for early-stage Web3 projects. Didn't ask for anything in return. Two years later, three of those projects had raised Series A. When he started his own company, those founders became his first angel investors and loudest advocates.

long_term_maintenance.title: Long-term Relationship Maintenance
long_term_maintenance.content:
Relationships decay without maintenance. Even strong relationships need periodic nurturing.

Maintenance strategies:

  • The quarterly check-in: Every 3 months, reach out to important connections with something valuable
  • Celebrate their wins: Congratulate them on launches, funding, or achievements
  • Remember details: Keep notes about their projects, interests, and goals. Reference them later
  • Share relevant content: When you see something they'd care about, send it their way
  • Meet in person when possible: Conferences are great for deepening online relationships

CRM for relationships: Use a simple system to track your network. A spreadsheet works. Track: Name, How you met, Last contact date, Notes about interests/projects, Next follow-up action.

Example tracking:
- Name: Alex Chen
- Met at: ETHDenver 2024
- Working on: DeFi protocol for emerging markets
- Last contact: Aug 15 (shared research paper)
- Next action: Check in when they launch mainnet (target: October)

reciprocity.title: Reciprocity in Web3
reciprocity.content:
Web3 culture is built on reciprocity and open collaboration. Understanding this is essential for successful networking.

How reciprocity works in Web3:

  • Open source mentality: People share knowledge freely and expect others to do the same
  • Pay it forward culture: Help others the way you were helped when you were starting
  • Reputation is everything: In a pseudonymous ecosystem, your reputation for being helpful carries immense weight
  • Network effects: The more you give, the stronger your network becomes

The compound interest of giving: When you help someone, they remember. They tell others. Those others reach out. You help them too. Eventually, your reputation as a helpful person becomes your strongest asset. When you need help, people come running.

Warning about over-giving: Give strategically, not indiscriminately. Your time is valuable. Help people who appreciate it and pay it forward themselves. Avoid energy vampires who only take.

The mutual respect principle: Both parties in a strong Web3 relationship bring value. If it's one-sided for too long, it's not sustainable. Aim for relationships where both people are genuinely useful to each other.

event_networking.title: Networking at Web3 Events
event_networking.content: Events and conferences are networking accelerators. You can accomplish in 3 days of in-person networking what might take 6 months online. But only if you approach them strategically.

conference_strategies.title: Conference Strategies (ETHDenver, Token2049, DevCon)
conference_strategies.content:
Major Web3 conferences draw thousands of attendees. Without a strategy, you'll waste time and energy. With a plan, you'll create opportunities that last for years.

Before the conference:

  • Set clear goals: What do you want to achieve? Meet 5 specific people? Find a co-founder? Learn about a technology?
  • Research attendees: Check speaker lists, sponsor lists, and social media. Make a target list of 10-20 people
  • Reach out in advance: DM your target connections: "Will you be at ETHDenver? Would love to meet up"
  • Schedule meetings: Book coffee chats or meals before slots fill up
  • Study the schedule: Prioritize talks and workshops. Don't try to attend everything

During the conference:

  • Quality over quantity: Better to have 5 deep conversations than 50 shallow ones
  • Be present in conversations: Put your phone away. Listen actively. Ask good questions
  • Take notes: After each conversation, write down key points and action items
  • Pace yourself: Conferences are exhausting. Don't burn out on day one
  • Go to side events: Often more valuable than the main conference (smaller, more focused)

At talks and panels: Sit near the front. Ask good questions during Q&A (brief, specific, adds to the discussion). Talk to speakers afterward—but wait for the crowd to thin.

hackathon_networking.title: Hackathon Networking
hackathon_networking.content:
Hackathons are unique networking environments. You're building together under time pressure—this creates deep bonds quickly.

Why hackathons are networking gold:

  • You see how people work under pressure
  • You build something together (shared experience)
  • Judges and sponsors are accessible
  • Winners get visibility and connections
  • Great for finding co-founders or early team members

Hackathon strategy:

  1. Form strategic teams: Join people whose skills complement yours. Mix developers, designers, and business people
  2. Network during formation: The team formation phase is when everyone is meeting people. Be proactive
  3. Engage with sponsors: Sponsors are often hiring or investing. Build in their tech stack. Talk to their team
  4. Present well: Your demo is your chance to impress judges, sponsors, and other hackers
  5. Stay in touch with teammates: Hackathon teammates often become co-founders, colleagues, or long-term collaborators

Real story: A developer went to ETHGlobal SF to learn. Teamed up with two strangers. They won a prize. Stayed in touch. Six months later, one teammate was fundraising and brought the other two in as co-founders. The company raised $5M seed. All from one hackathon.

side_events.title: Side Events and Dinners
side_events.content:
The "conference within the conference"—side events, dinners, and after-parties are often more valuable than the main event.

Types of side events:

  • Project-specific events: Individual protocols host their own meetups
  • Investor events: VCs host dinners and parties (harder to get into, but valuable)
  • Community meetups: Regional groups or interest groups (developers, designers, etc.)
  • Informal gatherings: Someone tweets "drinks at X bar at 8pm"—show up!

How to find side events:

  • Check lu.ma, Eventbrite, and conference Discord servers
  • Follow the conference hashtag on Twitter
  • Ask people you meet: "Going to any good side events?"
  • Check sponsor websites—they often list their events

Getting into exclusive events: Some events are invite-only or have limited capacity. How to get in:

  • Ask for invites from people who can bring guests
  • Engage with event organizers in advance on Twitter
  • Show up anyway if it's at a public venue (sometimes works for semi-private events)
  • Build relationships with community managers—they control invite lists

Making the most of small events: Intimate dinners with 10-20 people create the best connections. Everyone talks. You remember names. Real conversations happen. Prioritize these over massive parties.

virtual_events.title: Virtual Events and Twitter Spaces
virtual_events.content:
Can't travel to every conference? Virtual events and Twitter Spaces bring networking to you.

Twitter Spaces networking:

  • Participate as a speaker: Request to speak, ask questions, add insights. This gives you visibility
  • Engage in the chat: Even if not speaking, chat activity gets noticed
  • Follow up after: DM speakers or other participants: "Great point about X in the Space today"
  • Host your own: Hosting a Space positions you as a thought leader and connector

Virtual conference strategy:

  • Show up on video (not just audio)
  • Use chat actively—answer questions, share resources
  • Connect on Twitter/LinkedIn with people you meet
  • Join breakout rooms when available

The hybrid advantage: Virtual events lower the barrier. But in-person still wins for deep relationship building. Use virtual to expand your network broadly, use in-person to deepen key relationships.

post_event_followup.title: Post-Event Follow-up
post_event_followup.content:
The conference is over. This is where most people fail. The fortune is in the follow-up.

Within 24 hours:

  • Go through business cards or phone contacts
  • Write down who each person is and what you talked about (you'll forget quickly)
  • Send a brief message to each important connection: "Great meeting you at [Event]! Loved our conversation about [X]"

Within one week:

  • Deliver on any promises you made (intros, resources, etc.)
  • Share photos if you took any together
  • Connect on LinkedIn and Twitter if you haven't already
  • For key connections, suggest a follow-up call

Follow-up message template:
"Hey [Name], great meeting you at DevCon! Really enjoyed our conversation about [specific topic]. I mentioned [that resource/intro/etc]—here it is: [link]. Would love to stay in touch. Are you on Twitter? Let's connect."

What NOT to do: Don't immediately pitch your project or ask for favors. The follow-up should simply reinforce the connection and provide any value you promised.

The 3-month rule: Check in again in 3 months with something relevant. This transforms a conference handshake into an ongoing relationship.

online_presence.title: Building Your Online Presence
online_presence.content: In Web3, your online presence IS your reputation. Before anyone takes a meeting with you, they'll check your Twitter, GitHub, or LinkedIn. What they find determines whether they respond to your DM.

building_credibility.title: Building Credibility Before Reaching Out
building_credibility.content:
The best time to start networking is before you need it. When people can see your track record, they take you seriously.

Public proof of work:

  • Twitter thread about your learning: Document your journey learning a technology
  • GitHub contributions: Open source work is public credibility
  • Blog posts or articles: Share what you've learned
  • Project launches: Even small projects show you ship
  • Community contributions: Help others in Discord, answer questions

The credibility ladder:

  1. Complete beginner (asking basic questions)
  2. Learning in public (sharing your learning journey)
  3. Contributing value (helping others learn)
  4. Creating original content (threads, articles, tools)
  5. Recognized contributor (people seek your insights)

How to climb: Spend 30 minutes daily on public contributions. In 6 months, you'll have built significant credibility. When you reach out to someone, they'll see a history of valuable contributions.

Example: A developer wanted to connect with core Ethereum developers. Instead of cold DMing them, he spent 3 months: writing detailed threads explaining EIPs, contributing to documentation, answering beginner questions in forums. After 3 months, when he reached out to core devs, they already knew his name. Several responded within hours.

public_contributions.title: Public Contributions (Open Source, Content, Research)
public_contributions.content:
Public contributions are the currency of reputation in Web3. The more you give to the ecosystem, the more the ecosystem gives back.

Open source contributions:

  • Code: Fix bugs, add features, improve documentation in projects you use
  • Documentation: Many projects desperately need better docs
  • Translation: Help projects reach global audiences
  • Testing: Find and report bugs (responsibly)
  • Review: Review PRs, provide constructive feedback

Content creation:

  • Educational content: Tutorials, explainers, guides for beginners
  • Technical deep dives: Detailed analysis of protocols or technologies
  • Research synthesis: Summarize complex research papers for broader audiences
  • Thread summaries: Summarize conference talks or long-form content

Research contributions:

  • Original research on protocols, economics, or security
  • Data analysis and visualization
  • Benchmark studies
  • Threat models and security analysis

The compound effect: Each contribution is a node in your reputation graph. Over time, they connect. People discover your work, share it, and you become known for your area of expertise.

thought_leadership.title: Thought Leadership Positioning
thought_leadership.content:
Thought leadership isn't about having all the answers. It's about asking good questions, sharing insights, and moving conversations forward.

What thought leadership looks like in Web3:

  • Original insights: Your unique perspective on industry trends
  • Contrarian takes: Well-reasoned opinions that challenge consensus (when you're right)
  • Synthesis: Connecting dots that others miss
  • Prediction: Making specific, falsifiable predictions about the future
  • Analysis: Deep dives into events, protocols, or phenomena

How to develop your voice:

  1. Find your niche: What are you uniquely positioned to talk about?
  2. Have strong opinions, loosely held: Take positions, but change your mind with new evidence
  3. Engage in debates: Thoughtfully disagree when you have a point
  4. Share your thinking process: Don't just share conclusions—show your work
  5. Be consistent: Post regularly in your area of focus

Building an audience: Thought leadership naturally attracts followers. The right followers—people interested in your niche—are more valuable than mass followers. 1,000 engaged followers in DeFi beat 100,000 random crypto followers.

Authenticity matters: Don't fake expertise. If you're learning, say so. If you're uncertain, acknowledge it. Web3 Twitter is very good at detecting and punishing inauthenticity.

being_discoverable.title: Being Discoverable
being_discoverable.content:
The best opportunities often come from inbound—people discovering you. Make it easy for them to find you and understand what you do.

Optimize your profiles:

  • Twitter bio: Clear description of what you do + what you're interested in. Include relevant keywords
  • LinkedIn headline: More than just a job title—highlight your expertise
  • GitHub profile: Pin your best repositories. Write good READMEs
  • Personal website/portfolio: Centralize your work and make it easy to explore

Content discoverability:

  • Use relevant hashtags on Twitter (but don't overdo it)
  • Tag people and projects you mention (they'll often retweet)
  • Post in relevant subreddits and forums
  • Submit your work to newsletters and aggregators

SEO for your name: When someone Googles your name, what appears? Make sure your best work ranks high. This means: Using your real name (or consistent pseudonym), Publishing on platforms with high domain authority, Linking your various profiles together.

Example discoverable profile:
Twitter bio: "Researching MEV on L2s | Previously @EthereumFoundation | Writing at [blog].com"
Pinned tweet: Thread summarizing your best work
Recent tweets: Mix of original insights, retweets with commentary, and engagement
GitHub: Pinned repos showing your best projects
Result: When someone hears about you or sees your reply, they can instantly understand who you are and what you're about.

vcs_investors.title: Working with VCs and Investors
vcs_investors.content: If you're building a project, eventually you'll need to work with investors. The founder-investor relationship is a long-term partnership—choose wisely and build relationships before you need the money.

how_vcs_evaluate.title: How VCs Evaluate Founders
how_vcs_evaluate.content:
VCs invest in people as much as ideas. Understanding their evaluation criteria helps you build the right relationships.

What VCs look for in founders:

  • Founder-market fit: Do you have unique insight or experience in this market?
  • Execution ability: Track record of shipping and getting things done
  • Vision: Can you articulate a compelling 10-year vision?
  • Coachability: Can you take feedback and adapt?
  • Resilience: Startups are brutal—can you handle setbacks?
  • Team: Have you attracted strong co-founders and early employees?
  • Traction: Evidence the market wants what you're building

How VCs evaluate during meetings:

  • Your pitch clarity and storytelling ability
  • How you answer questions (especially hard ones)
  • Your depth of knowledge about the market and competitors
  • How you handle pushback or criticism
  • Your passion and commitment level

Red flags VCs watch for:

  • Defensiveness when questioned
  • Lack of self-awareness about weaknesses
  • Dishonesty or exaggeration
  • Not knowing your metrics
  • Bad-mouthing competitors or previous investors
  • Team conflicts or co-founder issues

getting_warm_intros.title: Getting Warm Intros to Investors
getting_warm_intros.content:
Cold emails to VCs have < 1% response rates. Warm intros have 50%+ response rates. The path to fundraising starts with building the right network.

Who can give you warm intros to VCs:

  • Portfolio company founders: VCs trust their portfolio companies' recommendations
  • Other VCs: VCs who passed but liked you will often intro to others
  • Successful founders: Even if not in that VC's portfolio, founder endorsements carry weight
  • Limited Partners (LPs): If you know someone who invests in the VC fund
  • Advisors and mentors: People in the ecosystem who know you well

Building relationships with portfolio company founders:

  1. Research the VC's portfolio
  2. Find companies in similar or adjacent spaces
  3. Reach out to founders for advice (not intro—yet)
  4. Build genuine relationship over time
  5. When appropriate, ask: "Do you think [VC] would be interested in what we're building?"

How to ask for an investor intro:
"Hey [Name], we're raising a $2M seed round for [company]. Based on what we're building, I think [VC Firm] could be a great fit because [specific reason]. I saw they invested in your company. Would you be comfortable making an introduction? No pressure if the timing isn't right. I've drafted a short blurb below to make it easy: [Draft]"

The draft forwardable intro: Make it easy for your connector. Provide 2-3 paragraphs they can forward: who you are, what you're building, why it's interesting, traction, and the ask.

what_investors_look_for.title: What Investors Actually Look For
what_investors_look_for.content:
Beyond the pitch deck, here's what investors really evaluate:

Traction and momentum:

  • Product-market fit signals: Organic growth, user retention, testimonials
  • Team momentum: Ability to recruit top talent
  • Capital efficiency: How much you've accomplished with limited resources
  • Velocity: How fast you ship and iterate

Market understanding:

  • Deep knowledge of customer pain points
  • Understanding of competitive landscape
  • Awareness of regulatory environment
  • Realistic TAM (Total Addressable Market) calculation

Network and deal flow:

  • VCs see hundreds of deals. They're pattern matching against what they've seen
  • Being recommended by trusted sources puts you in a different category
  • Multiple VCs talking about you creates FOMO

The intangibles:

  • Chemistry: VCs invest in founders they want to work with for 7-10 years
  • Storytelling: Can you make them believe in the vision?
  • X-factor: Something unique that makes you memorable

Crypto-specific factors:

  • Token economics understanding
  • Regulatory awareness
  • Community building ability
  • Understanding of crypto-native go-to-market

building_relationships_before_fundraisin.title: Building Relationships Before Fundraising
building_relationships_before_fundraisin.content:
The best time to start building investor relationships is 6-12 months before you need to raise. When VCs have watched your progress over time, they're far more likely to invest.

The relationship-building timeline:

  1. 12 months before raise: Start engaging with target VCs on Twitter. Share your progress publicly
  2. 9 months before: Reach out for advice (not money). "We're working on X, would love your thoughts on Y"
  3. 6 months before: Share milestone updates. "Thought you'd be interested—we just hit [metric]"
  4. 3 months before: Give them a heads up you'll be raising soon. "We're planning to raise in Q2"
  5. Raise time: They've watched your journey. They're pre-sold. Close becomes much easier

Update strategy: Send quarterly or milestone-based updates to investors you're building relationships with. Keep them concise:

  • What you've shipped
  • Key metrics
  • What you've learned
  • What's next

Don't ask for advice you won't take: If you ask for feedback, actually consider it. VCs notice if you ignore their input. But also don't blindly follow every suggestion—having conviction is important too.

Real example: Founder started tweeting their building journey 18 months before fundraising. Engaged thoughtfully with VCs on Twitter. When they launched, had 50K users in 3 weeks. When they announced fundraising, 15 VCs reached out inbound. Closed $5M seed in 2 weeks from VCs who had been following the journey.

team_building.title: Team Building and Hiring in Web3
team_building.content: Your team is your competitive advantage. In Web3's competitive talent market, hiring well is about network and reputation.

finding_cofounders.title: Finding Co-founders
finding_cofounders.content:
Co-founder relationships are like marriages. You'll spend more time with co-founders than family. Choose very carefully.

Where to find potential co-founders:

  • Hackathons: Work together under pressure. See compatibility and skills
  • Online communities: Discord servers, Telegram groups for builders
  • Previous colleagues: People you've worked with successfully before
  • School/university: Friends from your program (especially technical programs)
  • Open source: Contributors to projects you care about

What to look for in a co-founder:

  • Complementary skills: You need different strengths that combine well
  • Shared values: Alignment on ethics, culture, and long-term vision
  • Work compatibility: Work together on a project before committing
  • Resilience: Startups test mental fortitude—choose someone who won't quit
  • Trust: Can you trust them with everything? If not, don't do it

The dating period: Don't commit immediately. Work on a side project together for 2-3 months. Go to a hackathon together. See how you handle disagreements. Only then formalize the co-founder relationship.

Red flags:

  • Can't commit full-time when needed
  • Defensive about feedback
  • Different risk tolerance
  • Different expectations about equity, roles, or exit
  • History of leaving projects unfinished

The co-founder agreement: Once you commit, document everything: equity split, vesting schedule, roles and responsibilities, decision-making process, what happens if someone wants to leave.

hiring_in_web3.title: Hiring in Web3
hiring_in_web3.content:
Web3 hiring is different. Top talent has options. They're choosing between your startup, working at a protocol, or building their own thing.

How to attract top talent:

  • Mission and vision: Top people want to work on important problems
  • Learning and growth: Show how they'll level up working with you
  • Team quality: Highlight other strong people on the team
  • Ownership: Generous equity and real responsibility
  • Flexibility: Remote work, flexible hours, async communication
  • Reputation: Work that will enhance their personal brand

Where to find Web3 talent:

  • Community Discord servers: Protocol communities are full of engaged builders
  • Hackathons: Recruit winners and strong participants
  • Twitter: Developers ship in public. Find them via their work
  • GitHub: Contributors to relevant open source projects
  • Web3 job boards: crypto.jobs, web3.career, etc.
  • Referrals: Your team's network (offer referral bonuses)

The hiring process:

  1. Values screening: Do they care about your mission?
  2. Skills assessment: Can they do the work? (paid work trial > interviews)
  3. Culture fit: Will they thrive in your environment?
  4. Sell the opportunity: Remember, they're evaluating you too

Crypto-specific hiring considerations:

  • Remote-first is standard. Build processes for it
  • Token compensation can be powerful (if you have a token)
  • Many top devs prefer contract/part-time to start
  • Pseudonymous contributors can be excellent hires

building_network_for_hiring.title: Building Your Network for Future Hiring
building_network_for_hiring.content:
When you need to hire urgently, it's too late to start building relationships. Build your hiring pipeline continuously.

Creating a talent network:

  • Hackathon recruiting: Even if not hiring now, collect contacts from strong hackers
  • Open source community: Build relationships with contributors to your dependencies
  • Content creation: When you create valuable content, talented people reach out to you
  • Events and conferences: Meet people doing interesting work
  • Former colleagues: Maintain relationships with people you've enjoyed working with

The talent CRM: Keep a database of people you'd love to work with someday:

  • Name and contact
  • Skills and strengths
  • Where you met / how you know them
  • Why you'd want to work together
  • Last contact date
  • Next follow-up action

Staying top of mind: When you have an opening, you want talented people to think of you. How to stay visible:

  • Share company updates and wins on Twitter
  • Write about what you're building and why
  • Highlight team members' accomplishments
  • Be known as a great place to work

The boomerang effect: Some people you meet aren't ready to join now. Maybe they're at another company or still learning. Stay in touch. Check in every 6 months. When they're ready for their next thing, you're top of mind.

reference_checking.title: Reference Checking in a Pseudonymous World
reference_checking.content:
In Web3, many talented people work pseudonymously or have limited traditional work history. How do you validate talent and character?

Alternative reference checks:

  • Public work history: GitHub contributions, published articles, Twitter presence
  • Community reputation: Ask around in Discord/Telegram communities they're active in
  • On-chain history: For some roles, on-chain behavior shows competence and integrity
  • Previous projects: What have they built? Can you talk to those teams?
  • Hackathon teammates: Reach out to people they've worked with at hackathons

Red flags in Web3 reference checking:

  • No public work or GitHub contributions (for developer roles)
  • Negative sentiment in communities they've been part of
  • Burned bridges with previous projects
  • Inconsistencies in their story
  • Can't provide anyone who will vouch for them

The paid trial: For critical roles, especially with pseudonymous candidates, do a paid 2-4 week trial project. This reveals more than any interview or reference check.

Working with anons: Some of Web3's best talent is pseudonymous. Can you trust them?

  • Long-standing pseudonyms with reputation are safer than brand new accounts
  • On-chain identity tools (Proof of Humanity, ENS, etc.) add some verification
  • Smart contracts can help with trustless compensation arrangements
  • Start with smaller responsibilities, earn trust over time

Building trust gradually: In a pseudonymous ecosystem, trust is earned through repeated positive interactions. Don't expect instant trust—build it incrementally.

networking.definition: The process of building and maintaining professional relationships that can lead to opportunities, collaboration, and mutual support in the Web3 ecosystem.

cold_dm.definition: A direct message sent to someone you don't have an existing relationship with. In Web3, cold DMs should be personalized, provide value, and make a specific, easy-to-fulfill ask.

warm_intro.definition: An introduction made by a mutual connection who knows both parties. Far more effective than cold outreach, especially for investor or partnership conversations.

deal_flow.definition: The rate at which investment opportunities come to an investor. VCs with good deal flow see the best startups early. Being in someone's deal flow means they consider you for opportunities.

portfolio_company.definition: A company that a VC or investor has invested in. Portfolio companies can be valuable sources of warm introductions to their investors.

angel_investor.definition: An individual who invests their own money in early-stage startups. Angels often invest in pre-seed or seed rounds and can be more accessible than institutional VCs.

syndicate.definition: A group of investors who pool resources to invest together. In Web3, syndicates allow smaller investors to participate in deals alongside experienced leads.

founder_market_fit.definition: When a founder has unique insights, skills, or experience that make them exceptionally suited to build in their chosen market. VCs heavily weight this in investment decisions.

thought_leadership.definition: Establishing yourself as an expert and trusted voice in a specific domain through insightful content, original research, or valuable contributions to industry conversations.

personal_brand.definition: Your reputation and how you're perceived in the industry. In Web3, your personal brand is built through public contributions, consistent quality work, and how you interact with the community.

community_builder.definition: Someone who creates and nurtures communities around projects, protocols, or ideas. In Web3, strong community builders are highly valued for their ability to drive adoption and engagement.

ecosystem.definition: The network of projects, developers, users, and infrastructure built around a particular blockchain or protocol. Being well-connected in an ecosystem creates significant opportunities.

builder.definition: In Web3 culture, someone who creates products, protocols, or tools rather than just speculating. Being known as a builder carries significant social capital in the ecosystem.
